Commission Agenda Report
DATE:  September 9, 2026
TO:  Planning Commission
FROM:  Eric Scherer, Community Development Director
SUBJECT:  CASE NUMBER 75-26CUP – 2325 D STREET– CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT
  FOR AN ABC TYPE 41 BEER & WINE BEER AND WINE LICENSE FOR
  TACOS LA VILLA

SUMMARY
The applicant, Alexandra Bautista-Abad, doing business as Tacos La Villa, is requesting
approval for a Conditional Use Permit to obtain an Alcoholic Beverage Control (ABC) Type 41
beer and wine license in conjunction with a full-service sit-down Mexican restaurant located at
2325 D Street in Old Town La Verne. The restaurant is located within the Old Town La Verne
Specific Plan zone which requires approval of a Conditional Use Permit for the on-site sale of
beer and wine.

RECOMMENDATION
It is recommended that the Planning Commission:
1. Affirm CEQA Guidelines section 15301 (Class 1) (a) from the California Environmental
Quality Act based on this staff report and the findings and conditions of approval contained in
the attached resolution (Attachment 1).
2.Approve Case No. 75-26CUP by adopting Resolution No. 1361.

DISCUSSION
BACKGROUND
Tacos La Villa is a full-service sit-down Mexican restaurant offering breakfast, lunch and dinner,
as well as non-alcoholic beverages. The owners of Tacos La Villa have years of experience,
most recently operating in Bakersville before moving to La Verne.

Tacos La Villa is located at 2325 D Street, in Old Town La Verne, which is within the Old Town
La Verne Specific Plan zone. In May 2023, this location was occupied by Around the Grille for
about a year. Tacos La Villa has been in operation at this location since October of 2024 and
are now requesting to serve beer and wine at the restaurant.

The Old Town La Verne Specific Plan zone permits the on-site sale of beer and wine in
conjunction with an eating establishment when a Conditional Use Permit has been granted. All
restaurants with on-site sales of beer and wine must comply with California Alcoholic Beverage
Control (ABC) regulations and the sale of beer and wine must be incidental to that of food
service.

PROPOSAL

  Page 7 of 346
   CASE NO. 75-26CUP - CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT FOR AN ABC TYPE 41 BEER AND WINE LICENSE FOR TACOS LA
  VILLA, Page 2

The applicant is proposing beer and wine in conjunction with their food service under the
privileges of a Type 41 license, which authorizes the holder to sell beer & wine for on-site
consumption. The business must maintain suitable kitchen facilities and must make actual and
substantial sales of meals for consumption on the premises. A Type 41 license also allows
minors to be on the premises.

The restaurant’s hours of operation are 9 a.m. to 12 a.m., 7 days a week. There are 9
employees, and approximately 3 employees are on the premises at any given time. As they
offer a substantial food/meal menu, the proposed beer and wine service will be incidental and
secondary to the primary restaurant use. Tacos La Villa proposes to continue serving the City
as a neighborhood dining establishment focused on quality food, customer service, and a
welcoming atmosphere for families. The restaurant will maintain compliance with all applicable
state and local regulations, including the requirements of ABC, the LA County Health
Department, building & safety occupancy limitations and public safety standards.

The La Verne Municipal Code limits business operating hours to between 6:00 a.m. and 12:00
a.m. (midnight). Tacos La Villa currently operates from 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 a.m., Monday through
Sunday, which is consistent with the City’s permitted hours of operation. The California
Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control (ABC) allows the sale and service of alcoholic
beverages between 6:00 a.m. and 2:00 a.m. Tacos La Villa’s proposed beer and wine service
hours are also consistent with ABC regulations. However, to ensure consistency with the City’s
permitted business hours, staff has included a condition of approval limiting both restaurant
operations and beer and wine sales to between 6:00 a.m. and 12:00 a.m. (midnight) daily.

COMPATIBILITY WITH SURROUNDING USES
Tacos La Villa is located in Old Town La Verne, to the east of the University of La Verne. Within
the same area, there are a variety of land uses including various food establishments such as
Café Wang, Roberta’s and Warehouse Pizza, office/retail shops, and the University of La
Verne. The surrounding land uses include residential to the north across Bonita Avenue,
University of La Verne to the south, and similar commercial uses to the east and west.

The City of La Verne Police Department has not expressed any concern with the applicants’
proposed request to operate with this Type 41 license.

A notice of public hearing was published in the Inland Valley Daily Bulletin on August 25th,
2026, and notices were posted at City Hall, on the City’s website and mailed to all property
owners within 300 feet of the subject property on August 26th, 2026. Staff have not received any
inquiries about the proposal.

CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT FINDINGS
Approval of the Conditional Use Permit requires that the Commission make five specific
findings. These findings are set forth in this report’s Attachment 1, Resolution No. 1361, and the
analysis is incorporated by reference.

ENVIRONMENTAL ANALYSIS

  Page 8 of 346
   CASE NO. 75-26CUP - CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT FOR AN ABC TYPE 41 BEER AND WINE LICENSE FOR TACOS LA
  VILLA, Page 3

This project is categorically exempt from CEQA pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15301(a)
(Class 1). The Class 1 exemption is for existing facilities and subsection (a) speaks to the
example of interior or exterior alterations involving such things as tenant improvements. The
proposed project will be located in an existing building; there are no interior or exterior
improvements proposed as part of the project. The CEQA exemption is subject to the
exceptions of CEQA Guidelines section 15300.2. None of the exceptions would apply as there
are no successive projects of the same type in the same area that would create a cumulative
impact; there are no reasonable possibilities of a significant impact from the reuse of an existing
building; the project will not have any impacts to scenic highways as it does not involve any new
construction; the site is not a hazardous waste site; and the project does not involve any
historical resource. No further environmental review is required at this time.

ATTACHMENTS
1.  Resolution No. 1361
2.  Narrative
3.  Floor Plan

Valerie Chin, Assistant Planner

   RESOLUTION NO. 1361

A RESOLUTION OF THE PLANNING COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF LA VERNE,
COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES, STATE OF CALIFORNIA, APPROVING CASE NO. 75-
26CUP, A CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT TO ALLOW THE SALE AND ON-SITE
CONSUMPTION OF BEER AND WINE UNDER THE PRIVILEGES OF A TYPE 41
LIQUOR LICENSE AT THE RESTAURANT, TACOS LA VILLA, LOCATED AT 2325 D
STREET, AND FINDING THAT THE PROJECT IS EXEMPT FROM THE CALIFORNIA
ENVIRONMENTAL QUALITY ACT PER CEQA GUIDELINES SECTION 15301 (CLASS
1) (A).

  WHEREAS, on July 13, 2026, Alexandra Bautista-Abad DBA Tacos La Villa
submitted an application requesting a Conditional Use Permit to allow the sale and on-
site consumption of beer and wine under the privileges of a Type 41 Liquor License at
Tacos La Villa located at 2325 D Street; and

  WHEREAS, the Old Town La Verne Specific Plan, and Chapter 18.80 of the La
Verne Municipal Code requires a conditional use permit for this purpose; and

  WHEREAS, Sections 18.108.010 through 18.108.180 of the La Verne Municipal
Code authorizes the Planning Commission to consider such requests subject to certain
findings; and

  WHEREAS, a notice of public hearing was published in the Inland Valley Daily
Bulletin on August 25, 2026, and copies of the notice mailed to all property owners
within 300 feet of the subject property on August 25, 2026; and

  WHEREAS, the Planning Commission conducted a duly noticed public hearing
on September 9, 2026, at which time it considered all evidence presented, both written
and oral;

  NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the Planning Commission of the City
of La Verne:

  Section 1. Environmental Determination. The Planning Commission HEREBY
FINDS and DETERMINES that Case No. 75-26CUP, an application for a Conditional
Use Permit to allow to a conditional use permit for a Type 41 liquor license for the
business, Tacos La Villa, is exempt from CEQA based on the following.

This project is categorically exempt from CEQA pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section
15301(a) (Class 1). The Class 1 exemption is for existing facilities and subsection (a)
speaks to the example of interior or exterior alterations involving such things as tenant
improvements. The proposed project will be located in an existing building; there are no
interior or exterior improvements proposed as part of the project. The CEQA exemption
is subject to the exceptions of CEQA Guidelines section 15300.2. None of the exceptions
would apply as there are no successive projects of the same type in the same area that

 would create a cumulative impact; there are no reasonable possibilities of a significant
impact from the reuse of an existing building; the project will not have any impacts to
scenic highways as it does not involve any new construction; the site is not a hazardous
waste site; and the project does not involve any historical resource.

Additionally, the project is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act per
Section 15061(b)(3) in that the project/activity is not subject to CEQA due to the activity
being covered by the common sense exemption, which is that the activity in question
will not have any significant effect on the environment. This commonsense exemption
applies because there is no physical change to the building. No further environmental
review is required at this time. per CEQA Guidelines Section 15061(b)(3) under the
provisions of the California Environmental Quality Act, and no further environmental
review is necessary. The exemption is not subject to any of the exceptions set forth in
CEQA Guidelines Section 15

  Section 2. Findings. The Planning Commission HEREBY FINDS and
DETERMINES that the proposed Conditional Use Permit satisfies the findings of
Section 18.108.030 of the La Verne Municipal Code in that:

1.  The proposed use and development are each consistent with the general plan
  and the applicable land use zone.

  Finding: The proposed project is designated Specific Plan – Mixed Use by the
  La Verne General Plan and is located within the Old Town La Verne Specific
  Plan Zone. On-site sale of alcoholic beverages is identified as conditionally
  permitted use within the Old Town La Verne Specific Plan, and in conjunction
  with a bona fide restaurant in accordance with Chapter 18.80 of the La Verne
  Municipal Code.

2.  The site for the proposed use is adequate in size, shape, topography,
  accessibility, and other physical characteristics to accommodate the proposed
  use and development in a manner compatible with existing and proposed
  surrounding land uses.

  Finding: The site is already fully developed with the restaurant and is adequate
  in size, shape, topography and accessibility and other physical characteristics to
  accommodate the proposed use in a manner that is compatible with surrounding
  land uses.

3.  The development site has adequate access to those utilities and other services
  required for the proposed use.

  Finding: The site presently has adequate access to utilities and other services
  that are required for the proposed use, as evidenced by the fact that it is already
  developed with an existing restaurant use.

 4.  The proposed use will be arranged, designed, constructed, operated and
  maintained so as to be compatible with the character of the area as intended by
  the general plan.

  Finding: The proposed use is compatible with existing uses within the same
  shopping area, the greater Old Town La Verne Specific Plan area, and with those
  in the nearby surrounding areas. The use and all associated equipment and
  materials will be conducted and kept within the enclosed building. The conditions
  of approval will ensure that the potential impacts of the use on neighboring
  properties, such as noise, ensure compatibility with the neighborhood.

5.  Potential adverse effects upon the surrounding properties will be minimized to
  the extent practical and any remaining adverse effects are justified by the
  benefits conferred upon the neighborhood or community as a whole.

  Finding: It is not expected that there will be any adverse effects on the
  surrounding area. Any potential impacts will be addressed by conditions of
  approval. The proposed on-site sale of beer and wine serves a public
  convenience or necessity because it will offer an additional choice to La Verne
  residents and increase access to a broader array of products within the City.
  Beer and wine sales are an expected and ordinary activity associated with food
  sales.

  Section 3. Approval. In accordance with the provisions of the La Verne
Municipal Code, the Planning Commission HEREBY APPROVES Case No. 75-26CUP
and the accompanying environmental determination subject to the following conditions
of approval:

  1. Beer and wine sales shall be subject to approval by the Department of Alcoholic
  Beverage Control (ABC); all requirements of ABC shall be met. The applicant
  shall provide verification of ABC approval prior to the sale of any alcoholic
  beverages.

  2. The sale of beer and wine shall be incidental to the primary use as a bona fide
  restaurant as defined in the California Business and Professions code.

  3. The design of the facilities shall conform with all ABC regulations, and building
  permits shall be obtained prior to any tenant improvements/modifications that are
  ultimately required by ABC.

  4. The hours of operation for the restaurant, including the sales and on-site
  consumption of alcohol, shall be not be outside the hours of 6:00 a.m. and 12:00
  a.m. (midnight), seven days a week or in accord with ABC regulations if more
  restrictive.

  5. Operating procedures shall include the following:

SUBJECT:  CASE NUMBER 77-26CUP – 1275 FOOTHILL BOULEVARD – CONDITIONAL
  USE PERMIT TO MODIFY AN EXISTING LATE-NIGHT BUSINESS (CRUNCH
  FITNESS)

SUMMARY
The applicant, Jeff Jennings, doing business as Jplus Architects, is requesting approval for a
Conditional Use Permit to modify an existing permit for a late-night business for Crunch Fitness
located at 1275 Foothill Boulevard. The gym is located within the Foothill Boulevard Specific
Plan zone which requires approval of a Conditional Use Permit to operate late night businesses
within 300 feet of residential uses.

RECOMMENDATION
It is recommended that the Planning Commission:
1. Affirm an exemption from the California Environmental Quality Act per CEQA Guidelines
section 15301 (Class 1)(a) based on this staff report and the findings and conditions of approval
contained in the attached resolution (Attachment 1); and
2. Adopt Resolution No. 1362, approving Case No. 75-26CUP.

DISCUSSION
BACKGROUND
The Planning Commission previously approved the use of a gym at 1275 Foothill Boulevard in
1999 (Case No. 97-98CUP). This location was occupied by LA Fitness between 2001 and its
recent closure in April of 2026. Crunch Fitness will be the new tenant at this address, located in
the Gateway Pointe shopping center which is within the Foothill Boulevard Specific Plan zone.
Crunch Fitness is a full-service fitness club offering general workout areas, cardio equipment,
strength training equipment, and group fitness areas.

A Conditional Use Permit (CUP) is required by the Foothill Boulevard Specific Plan for
businesses operating between the hours of 12a.m. and 6a.m., less than 300 feet from
residential properties. LA Fitness was issued a CUP to operate between 12 a.m. and 4:30 a.m.
However, Crunch Fitness wishes to operate 24 hours a day and therefore needs a modification
of the late-night CUP to cover the additional hours of 4:30 a.m. to 6 a.m.

The building is approximately 300 feet away from the nearest residential uses, and the parcel
itself is about 50 feet away. The project site is approximately 41,000 square feet in size and has
historically operated as a fitness facility. The proposed 24-hour operation will allow the facility to
better serve residents and members with varied schedules who may not be able to use the
facility during traditional business hours.

  Page 17 of 346
   CASE NO. 77-26CUP - CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT TO MODIFY AN EXISTING LATE-NIGHT BUSINESS FOR CRUNCH
  FITNESS, Page 2

PROPOSAL
The applicant is proposing modified late night operation hours in conjunction with the fitness
facility, which will utilize the previously approved CUPs for LA Fitness for the gym (Case No. 97-
98CUP) and for late night hours between 12:00 a.m. and 4:30 a.m. (Case No. 117-00CUP). The
La Verne Municipal Code typically limits hours of operation for businesses to the hours of 6:00
a.m. and 12:00 a.m. (midnight). Crunch Fitness’ new proposed hours of operation are 24 hours
a day, 7 days a week.

Building permits for exterior and interior structural modifications to the tenant space have been
submitted and are currently under review, independent of this CUP request.

COMPATIBILITY WITH SURROUNDING USES
Crunch Fitness will be located in the Gateway Pointe Plaza shopping center which is on the
west side of Foothill Boulevard near the intersection of Wheeler Avenue and Foothill Boulevard.
Within the same shopping center there are a variety of uses, including quick service food
establishments such as Starbucks, IHOP, and Kaiba, and various hair and nail salons, as well
as office uses. The surrounding land uses include the 210 Freeway to the north, mobile home
parks to the south, and similar commercial uses to the east and west across Foothill Boulevard.

The City of La Verne Police Department has not expressed any concern with the applicant’s
proposed request to operate with the additional late-night hours. However, additional
precautions for increased lighting have been added as a condition of approval.

A notice of public hearing was published in the Inland Valley Daily Bulletin on August 25th,
2026, and notices were posted at City Hall, on the City’s website and mailed to all property
owners within 300 feet of the subject property on May 26th, 2026. Staff have not received any
inquiries about the proposal.

CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT FINDINGS
Approval of the Conditional Use Permit requires that the Commission make five specific
findings. These findings are set forth in Attachment 1, Resolution No. 1362, and the analysis is
incorporated by reference.

ENVIRONMENTAL ANALYSIS
This project is categorically exempt from CEQA pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15300.2.
None of the exceptions would apply as there are no successive projects of the same type in the
same area that would create a cumulative impact; there are no reasonable possibilities of a
significant impact from the reuse of an existing building; the project will not have any impacts to
scenic highways as it does not involve any new construction; the site is not a hazardous waste
site; and the project does not involve any historical resource. No further environmental review is
required at this time.

Project Intent
Crunch Fitness respectfully submits this request for a Conditional Use Permit to allow the fitness facility
located at 1275 Foothill Blvd, La Verne, CA 91750 to operate 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
The project site is the former LA Fitness location and is approximately 41,000 square feet. The site has
historically operated as a fitness facility and previously had approval to operate as early as 4:30 a.m. The
proposed request is to allow the continued fitness use with expanded hours of operation to provide 24-hour
access for members.
Crunch Fitness provides a welcoming, inclusive, and community-oriented fitness environment for members
of all fitness levels. The proposed 24-hour operation allows the facility to better serve residents and
members with varying schedules, including healthcare workers, public safety employees, shift workers,
commuters, parents, and others who may not be able to use the facility during traditional business hours.

Operations
The proposed operation is for a full-service fitness club offering general workout areas, cardio equipment,
strength training equipment, group fitness areas, locker rooms, and related fitness amenities. The use will
remain consistent with the prior fitness operation of the site.
The facility is proposed to operate 24 hours per day, 7 days per week. Staffing levels will vary based on the
time of day and member demand, with higher staffing levels during peak daytime and evening hours.
Overnight operations will be limited compared to daytime use and are expected to have lower member
traffic. Staff will be provided as needed to support operations, member assistance, security, and general
facility oversight.
The 24-hour operation is important to the Crunch Fitness business model and provides flexibility for
members who need access outside of standard operating hours. Because fitness facility usage is spread
throughout the day, 24-hour access can also help reduce the concentration of member traffic during peak
hours.

Security and Access Control
Security and member safety are important parts of the proposed 24-hour operation. Access to the facility will
be controlled and limited to members and authorized guests. The facility will utilize controlled entry points,
member check-in procedures, and security measures consistent with Crunch Fitness operations.
The site will be monitored and managed to maintain a safe environment for members, employees, and the
surrounding property. Any overnight access will be limited to authorized members, and the facility will
continue to follow internal operational procedures for security, emergency response, and member conduct.

Noise and Neighborhood Compatibility
The proposed 24-hour operation is not expected to create significant noise impacts. Fitness activities occur
inside the building, and no outdoor classes, outdoor amplified sound, or exterior workout activities are
proposed as part of this request.
The facility will operate in a manner that respects the surrounding commercial area and adjacent properties.
Interior music and activities will be managed so that noise does not create impacts beyond the tenant space.
The proposed use is consistent with the existing fitness nature of the site and will continue to function as an
indoor commercial fitness facility.

Parking and Traffic
The site was previously used as an LA Fitness facility, and the proposed Crunch Fitness use will continue
the same general fitness use of the property. The request is primarily related to expanding the allowed
operating hours to 24 hours.
Because member visits occur throughout the day and night, the 24-hour operation helps distribute activity
over a longer period rather than concentrating all use within limited daytime and evening hours. Overnight
use is typically lower than daytime and peak evening activity. The existing parking field serving the property
is expected to continue to support the fitness use.

Previous Operations History
The tenant space was formerly occupied by LA Fitness and has historically operated as a fitness facility. The
prior operation had a Conditional Use Permit allowing early morning operation beginning at 4:30 a.m. This
application requests approval to expand the permitted operating hours to allow 24-hour operation for Crunch
Fitness.

Community Benefit
The proposed Crunch Fitness will continue to provide a valuable health and wellness amenity for the La
Verne community. The 24-hour operation provides flexible access for members with nontraditional
schedules and supports a broad range of residents, workers, and families.
The project will also help reactivate and continue the productive use of an existing commercial fitness
facility. The proposed operation is compatible with the prior use of the site and supports continued
commercial activity within the existing shopping center.

Conclusion
Crunch Fitness respectfully requests approval of the Conditional Use Permit to allow 24-hour operation at
1275 Foothill Blvd, La Verne, CA 91750. The request supports the continued operation of an existing fitness
facility, provides expanded access for members, maintains appropriate security and operational controls,
and is compatible with the surrounding commercial setting.

Commission Agenda Report
DATE:  September 9, 2026
TO:  Planning Commission
FROM:  Eric Scherer, Community Development Director
SUBJECT:  2026 CITY OF LA VERNE LOCAL HAZARD MITIGATION PLAN AND
  GENERAL PLAN SAFETY ELEMENT AMENDMENT

SUMMARY
The Planning Commission will consider the 2026 City of La Verne Local Hazard Mitigation Plan
and a proposed amendment to the General Plan Safety Element incorporating the Plan by
reference. The Federal Emergency Management Agency has determined that the Local Hazard
Mitigation Plan is Approvable Pending Adoption. City Council adoption is required for final
approval and will maintain the City’s eligibility for certain federal hazard mitigation grant
programs. Staff also recommends incorporating the Local Hazard Mitigation Plan into the
General Plan Safety Element in accordance with Assembly Bill 2140, which may provide the
City with additional eligibility for State disaster-related funding. The Planning Commission is
being asked to recommend approval of both actions to the City Council.

RECOMMENDATION
It is recommended that the Planning Commission conduct the public hearing and adopt
Planning Commission Resolution No. 1363, recommending that the City Council:

  1. Adopt the 2026 City of La Verne Local Hazard Mitigation Plan; and
  2. Approve an amendment to the General Plan Safety Element incorporating the 2026
  Local Hazard Mitigation Plan by reference in accordance with Assembly Bill 2140.

The Planning Commission resolution would also recommend that the City Council find the
proposed actions exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act pursuant to California
Environmental Quality Act Guidelines Section 15061(b)(3).

DISCUSSION
In March 2025, the City of La Verne began updating its Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP) to
identify natural hazards, evaluate community vulnerabilities, and establish strategies to reduce
long-term risks to life and property. The La Verne Fire Department secured funding for
preparation of the LHMP through a Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Hazard
Mitigation Assistance Grant. The Plan was prepared in accordance with FEMA Region 9 and
the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services (Cal OES) guidelines. An 18-member
stakeholder Steering Committee oversaw preparation of the LHMP. The planning process also
included public outreach events, online information, surveys, and social media engagement.

The 2026 LHMP evaluates eight natural hazards considered significant to La Verne: dam
failure, drought, earthquake, extreme temperatures, extreme wind, flooding, landslides, and

  Page 49 of 346
  2026 CITY OF LA VERNE LOCAL HAZARD MITIGATION PLAN AND GENERAL PLAN SAFETY ELEMENT AMENDMENT,
  Page 2

wildfire. The LHMP establishes goals, strategies, and actions to reduce the City’s vulnerability
to these hazards and coordinate mitigation efforts among City departments.

On May 22, 2026, FEMA notified the City that the LHMP was Approvable Pending Adoption.
This determination means the Plan meets applicable federal planning requirements, subject to
formal adoption by the City Council. Following City Council adoption, documentation will be
submitted to FEMA for final approval. Final approval will maintain the City’s eligibility to apply for
certain federal hazard mitigation funding to implement eligible projects and strategies identified
in the LHMP. The LHMP will remain in effect for a five-year planning cycle and may be updated
as hazards, vulnerabilities, and mitigation priorities change.

GENERAL PLAN SAFETY ELEMENT AMENDMENT: Staff is also recommending an
amendment to the General Plan Safety Element to incorporate the 2026 LHMP. Assembly Bill
2140 (AB 2140) provides an incentive for cities and counties to incorporate a federally approved
local hazard mitigation plan into the Safety Element of their General Plan. Government Code
Section 8685.9 provides that, when these requirements are met, the Legislature may authorize
the State to pay more than 75 percent of eligible local disaster-related costs. The proposed
amendment is limited to incorporating the 2026 LHMP. It does not change land use
designations, development densities, zoning, or authorize development. The amendment will
better coordinate the City’s General Plan with its hazard mitigation and emergency
preparedness efforts and may provide additional financial assistance opportunities following a
declared disaster. Future updates to the LHMP will be coordinated with the General Plan Safety
Element as required by applicable State law.

GENERAL PLAN CONSISTENCY: The proposed amendment is consistent with the purpose
and intent of the General Plan because it supports existing policies related to public safety,
emergency preparedness, natural hazards, and community resiliency. By incorporating the
LHMP, the Safety Element will reflect the City’s updated hazard assessment and mitigation
strategies without changing existing land use policies or authorizing development. The Planning
Commission serves as the recommending body for General Plan amendments, with final action
taken by the City Council.

PUBLIC NOTICE: A Notice of Public Hearing was published in the Inland Valley Daily Bulletin
on August 26, 2026, for the September 9, 2026 Planning Commission hearing. The notice
identified the proposed 2026 LHMP and General Plan Safety Element amendment and provided
information for submitting public comments.

PLANNING COMMISSION ACTION: The Planning Commission will consider adoption of
Planning Commission Resolution No. 1363, recommending that the City Council adopt the 2026
LHMP and approve the related General Plan Safety Element amendment. If recommended by
the Planning Commission, the matter will proceed to a duly noticed City Council public hearing.
The City Council will consider two separate resolutions: one adopting the 2026 LHMP and one
approving the General Plan Safety Element amendment incorporating the LHMP by reference.

  WHEREAS, the LHMP was prepared in accordance with the federal Disaster
Mitigation Act of 2000 and applicable Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA)
and California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services guidelines; and

  WHEREAS, preparation of the LHMP included participation from City
departments, community stakeholders, and the public; and

  WHEREAS, the LHMP identifies and evaluates natural hazards affecting the City,
including dam failure, drought, earthquake, extreme temperatures, extreme wind,
flooding, landslides, and wildfire; and

  WHEREAS, on May 22, 2026, FEMA determined that the 2026 LHMP was
Approvable Pending Adoption, subject to formal adoption by the City Council; and

  WHEREAS, formal adoption of the LHMP will allow the City to maintain eligibility
to apply for certain federal hazard mitigation grant programs; and

  WHEREAS, Assembly Bill 2140 (AB 2140, 2006) provides an incentive for cities
and counties to incorporate a federally approved local hazard mitigation plan into the
Safety Element of their General Plan; and

  WHEREAS, AB 2140 provides that incorporation of a local hazard mitigation plan
into the General Plan Safety Element may allow the Legislature to authorize an
increased State share of eligible disaster-related costs; and

  WHEREAS, the proposed General Plan Safety Element amendment would
incorporate the 2026 LHMP by reference and does not change land use designations,
development densities, zoning, or authorize development; and

  WHEREAS, the proposed General Plan Safety Element amendment is
consistent with the purpose and intent of the General Plan because it supports existing
policies related to public safety, emergency preparedness, natural hazards, and
community resiliency; and

General Plan Safety Element amendment, and all written and oral testimony presented;

of La Verne as follows:

  Section 1. Incorporation of Recitals. The Recitals set forth above are incorporated
herein as findings of fact.

  Section 2. Findings: Based upon the staff report, the 2026 City of La Verne Local
Hazard Mitigation Plan, and the information presented at the public hearing, the Planning
Commission finds as follows:

  A. The City of La Verne is subject to natural hazards, including dam failure,
  drought, earthquake, extreme temperatures, extreme wind, flooding,
  landslides, and wildfire, that may pose risks to life, property, the environment,
  and the local economy.

  B. The 2026 LHMP provides a comprehensive framework for identifying these
  hazards, evaluating community vulnerabilities, and establishing strategies and
  actions to reduce long-term risks.

  C. Preparation of the LHMP included coordination among City departments,
  community stakeholders, and the public and was completed in accordance with
  applicable federal and State hazard mitigation planning guidelines.

  D. FEMA’s May 22, 2026 Approvable Pending Adoption determination confirms
  that the LHMP satisfies applicable federal planning requirements, subject to
  formal adoption by the City Council.

  E. Adoption of the LHMP will support the City’s hazard mitigation and emergency
  preparedness efforts and maintain eligibility to apply for certain federal hazard
  mitigation funding programs.

  F. Incorporating the LHMP by reference into the General Plan Safety Element will
  strengthen coordination between the City’s General Plan, hazard mitigation,
  and emergency preparedness efforts.

  G. The proposed General Plan Safety Element amendment is consistent with the
  purpose and intent of the General Plan because it supports existing policies

  H. The proposed amendment does not change land use designations,

  with Assembly Bill 2140 and may provide the City with additional eligibility for
  State disaster-related financial assistance.

  J. The adoption of the LHMP and General Plan Safety Element amendment is
  consistent with the goals, policies, purpose, and intent of the City of La Verne
  General Plan and will strengthen coordination between the City’s long-range
  planning, hazard mitigation, and emergency preparedness efforts.

  Section 3. Environmental Review. The Planning Commission recommends that
the City Council find that adoption of the 2026 City of La Verne Local Hazard Mitigation
Plan and the related General Plan Safety Element amendment are exempt from the
California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant to Sections 15061(b)(3) (Common
Sense Exemption) and 15262 (Feasibility and Planning Studies) of the State CEQA
Guidelines. The LHMP is a planning document that identifies natural hazard risks and
potential mitigation strategies. Adoption of the LHMP and its incorporation by reference
into the General Plan Safety Element do not commit the City to any specific future action,
development, construction, or physical improvement. It can be seen with certainty that
the proposed actions will not result in a significant effect on the environment. Any future
physical improvement or mitigation project identified in the LHMP will be subject to
separate environmental review under CEQA, as applicable. None of the exceptions under
Section 15300.2 of the State CEQA Guidelines apply.

incorporating the 2026 City of La Verne Local Hazard Mitigation Plan by reference in
accordance with Assembly Bill 2140.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

View Above the City of La Verne

Hazard mitigation involves implementing cost-effective and sustainable
measures to minimize the risk to human life, property, and infrastructure
from potential hazards. Through this mitigation plan, the City has developed
a framework to lessen the impacts of natural disasters and create a more
resilient community.

HAZARD MITIGATION OVERVIEW

The City of La Verne (City) is updating its local hazard mitigation plan (LHMP) to show its
commitment to reducing risk of hazards for the residents, assets, and community lifelines
within the City. This plan aims to safeguard the people and essential services provided
throughout the Planning Area.

The LHMP forms the foundation for the City’s long-term strategy to reduce disaster losses
and break the cycle of disaster damage, reconstruction, and repetitive damage. This plan
aligns with federal and state hazard mitigation planning regulations and requirements to
ensure the City is eligible for pre- and post-disaster mitigation funding through the Federal
Emergency Management Agency (FEMA).

PLANNING PROCESS

The planning process chapter of the mitigation plan highlights how the plan came together,
who was a part of the process, and what data and information were utilized to create or
revise the plan. A successful planning endeavor involves engaging with community leaders,
stakeholders, and the public to ensure their input and support throughout the process. For
this LHMP, Chapter 2 (Planning Process) documents the process the Steering Committee
followed to develop the 2026 City of La Verne LHMP update.

BUILDING THE PLANNING TEAMS

The City brought together a diverse and inclusive group of individuals to participate, develop,
and implement the LHMP. A Core Planning Team (CPT) and Steering Committee oversaw the
planning process and were responsible for coordinating, overseeing, and executing the
planning process.

1.  INTRODUCTION
1.1  WHY PREPARE THIS PLAN?

The City of La Verne prepared this Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP) to
better protect the residents, property, and assets throughout the City from
the effects of natural hazards.

View Above the City of La Verne

Hazard mitigation plays a crucial role in emergency management by working to reduce the
impacts of disasters on individuals, communities, and important assets. By implementing
mitigation measures, we can help prevent the same areas from being repeatedly impacted
by disasters. Mitigation is part of the emergency management cycle, which is divided into
four phases:

  •  Preparedness is when we develop or update activities, programs and systems before
  an event happens. These activities are often tested (or exercised) in non-emergency
  situations to determine their effectiveness. Emergency managers also assess
  potential risks, hazards, and vulnerabilities in this phase.
  •  Response focuses on the immediate and short-term effects of a disaster. It is usually
  focused on life safety and preventing immediate damage.

  1-1

  Page 88 of 346
   2026 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan | Introduction

  •  Recovery is a long-term phase that looks to return a community to normal, or to a
  more resilient state, after a disaster.
  •  Mitigation focuses on building (or rebuilding) in ways that reduce the risk more
  permanently. It is an activity that can occur at any point in the emergency
  management cycle. For example, communities can undertake mitigation actions
  before a disaster (the preparedness phase) or while rebuilding after a disaster (the
  recovery phase) (FEMA 2023).

 1.1.1  Federal Eligibility

Disaster Mitigation Act
In an effort to reduce the Nation's mounting natural disaster losses, the US Congress passed
the Disaster Mitigation Act of 2000 (DMA 2000), which amended the Robert T. Stafford
Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act. Section 322 of DMA 2000 emphasizes the need
for state and local government entities to closely coordinate on mitigation planning activities
and requires a hazard mitigation plan (HMP) for any local government applying for federal
mitigation grant funds. These funds primary fall under FEMA HMA program. Grant programs
under HMA include the following:

  •  Fire Management Assistance Grant.
  •  Flood Mitigation Assistance.
  •  Hazard Mitigation Grant Program.
  •  Rehabilitation of High Hazard Potential Dams (HHPD).
  •  Public Assistance – Categories C through G.

Entities with an adopted and federally-approved LHMP are pre-positioned to receive
available mitigation funds before and after the next disaster strikes. The plan was developed
to make La Verne eligible for pre- and post-disaster FEMA grants.

updated with a focus on assessing changes in vulnerability caused by hazard events,
evaluating capabilities and their utilization in implementing hazard mitigation measures,
reviewing the 2012 mitigation strategy, and identifying new initiatives to enhance overall
resilience in the City.

This plan update process has been treated as an initial planning effort due to the gap in plan
updates since 2012. This planning process was a functional reset of the mitigation strategies
for La Verne.

Federal and State Requirements
In response to the requirements of the DMA 2000, which requires local governmental
agencies to develop and update its HMP every 5 years, this plan serves as the 2026 update
to the 2012 City of La Verne Local Hazard Mitigation Plan. This update is in alignment with
FEMA’s Local Mitigation Planning Policy Guide (April 2025), FEMA’s Local Mitigation Planning
Handbook (June 2025), and the State of California planning requirements.

Changes in Hazards
The 2012 LHMP assessed Earthquake, Earth Movement (Landslide/Debris Flow), Flood, Wildfire,
and Windstorm. This update expands on those hazards by also assessing Dam Failure,
Drought, and Extreme Temperature.

3.  CITY OF LA VERNE PROFILE
This chapter provides general information about the City of La Verne, including its historical
information, physical setting, general building stock, land use, population, demographics,
population trends, and community lifelines. Analyzing this information leads to an
understanding of the study area, including economic, structural, and population assets at
risk, and of concerns that could be related to hazards analyzed in this plan (e.g., low-lying
areas prone to flooding, high percentage of vulnerable persons in an area).

3.1  OVERVIEW

 3.1.1  Historical Overview

According to the La Verne Historical Society, due to its flourishing citrus industry, La Verne a
a destination for migrant labor in the early 20th century. Nationalities that immigrated to La
Verne included Mexican, Chinese, Indian, Japanese, andFilipino immigrants. Mexican immig
rants who settled in La Verne after 1910 lived south of the Santa Fe railroad tracks in the and
worked extensively in the orange groves and packing houses (City of La Verne 2022).

La Verne was incorporated in 1906 following a period of land speculation brought on by the
extension of the Santa Fe Railroad. Originally named Lordsburg at the time of its founding in
1887, the City was selected as the site of the University of La Verne, which was established in
1892 and remains an important community institution. The City was known as the “Heart of
the Orange Empire” due to its flourishing citrus industry, until rapid post-WWII development
shaped the City’s residential neighborhoods (City of La Verne 2025).

The foothills of the San Gabriel Mountains north of Baseline Road were settled by ranchers in
the late 1800s and early 1900s. Meanwhile, the Lordsburg (what will eventually become Old
Town La Verne) sprung up along the extension of the Santa Fe Railroad in the southern half
of modern day La Verne. These ranches in the north became productive agricultural groves
during the citrus boom of the early 1900s. After World War II, the demand for residential
development led citrus farmers to sell their agricultural land for housing developments. The
large parcels were typically sold and developed with single-family subdivisions, fueling
population growth during the 1970s and 1980s. Market conditions at the time, in addition to
the steep hilly terrain (many areas of north La Verne have a slop of 20% or greater) and
environmental and safety constraints (including fire hazard concerns), led to almost all prior
citrus farms land being developed with lower-density, single-family housing which could
most feasibility fit within the unique hilly topography of this part of the City (City of La Verne
2022).

 3.1.2  Government

The City of La Verne is governed by a council-manager form of government, where a five-
member City Council, elected by district, makes policy decisions, and a City Manager,
appointed by the council, oversees daily operations. The City Council will assume the
responsibility for the adoption of this local hazard mitigation plan while the City Manager will
be responsible for overseeing its implementation.

The City of La Verne, California, provides a wide array of services, including community
development, parks and recreation, public works, fire, and police.

3.2  PHYSICAL SETTING

This section describes the location, geography, topography, watersheds, and climate of the
City of La Verne.

 3.2.1  Location

The City of La Verne is nestled in the scenic foothills of the San Gabriel Mountains
approximately 35 miles east of Los Angeles, with an area of approximately nine square miles.
The City is bounded by San Dimas to the west, Claremont to the east, Pomona to the south,
and the San Gabriel Mountains to the north.

 3.2.2  Geology, Geography, and Topography

The city is situated at the base of the San Gabriel Mountains, which are part of the Angeles
National Forest. Elevations in the City range from a high of 1,700 feet to a low of 1,000 feet. The
terrain of the city is a combination of relatively flat land in the mid and southern portions and
hills primarily in the northern half of the City.

Geologically, La Verne is part of the larger San Gabriel Valley region, which is an alluvial plain
created by the weathering of the San Gabriel Mountains. The plain slopes generally to the
southeast at about 1.05 feet for every 100 feet. Soils in the San Gabriel Valley consist of alluvial
debris deposited from the weathering of the San Gabriel Mountains and generally consist of
sand, gravel, and clay deposited in successive layers by runoff from the nearby mountains
and hills.

The San Dimas Creek system, most of which is in the City of San Dimas to the west, is the

(City of La Verne 2012).

 3.2.4  Climate

The climate of the City of La Verne is typical of Southern California with generally mild
temperatures and little to no days below freezing. Average temperatures in the City of La
Verne range from 55 degrees Fahrenheit in the winter months to 72 degrees Fahrenheit in the
summer months. However, the temperatures can vary over a wide range, particularly when
the Santa Ana winds blow, bringing higher temperatures and very low humidity.
Temperatures rarely exceed 110 degrees Fahrenheit in the summer months (June -
September), and rarely drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit in the winter months (November-
March).

3.3  POPULATION AND DEMOGRAPHICS

Those that live in the City are one of the most important assets and this LHMP will assess risk
to people and identify mitigation strategies to protect them, including equity priority
populations.

 3.3.1  General Population

Although La Verne is located in metropolitan Los Angeles County, it is a "close-knit"
community that has been able to retain its "small town" traditions and virtues. With eight
mobile home parks and three large retirement communities, La Verne has a significant senior
citizen population. In addition, due to an influx of new upscale housing during the past two
decades, La Verne also enjoys a large clientele of school-age youth. La Verne is a well-
balanced residential community that includes a good mix of commercial and industrial uses
as well as the University of La Verne, an airport, and fine public and private schools (City of
La Verne 2025).

  3.3.2  Vulnerable Populations

Underserved communities are populations sharing a particular characteristic, as well as
geographic communities, which have been systematically denied a full opportunity to
participate in aspects of economic, social, and civic life. Social vulnerability is the potential
for loss within an individual or social group. The term recognizes that some traits influence
an individual’s or group’s resilience. This is their ability to prepare, respond, cope or recover
from an event (FEMA 2023).

Underserved communities and socially vulnerable populations located within the jurisdiction
may be more at-risk during hazard events due to a variety of factors, such as their physical
and financial capacity to react or respond effectively, as well as the location and quality of

their housing. Those with greater vulnerability may experience more severe impacts during
emergencies or disasters. It is essential for public officials to consider the distinct needs of
vulnerable populations in order to ensure their safety.

Social Vulnerability Index
The CDC SVI is a place-based index, database, and mapping application designed to identify
and quantify communities experiencing social vulnerability. The current CDC SVI uses 16 US
census variables from the 5-year American Community Survey to identify communities that
may need support before, during, or after disasters. The factors include economic data as
well as data regarding education, family characteristics, housing, language ability, ethnicity,
and vehicle access. These variables are combined into a single measure of overall social
vulnerability (CDC/ATSDR 2024). The Steering Committee chose this dataset as the basis for
defining vulnerable populations or “equity priority communities” in this plan. Factors from the

The Steering Committee identified the following socially vulnerable populations and
underserved communities within the City of La Verne and prioritized understanding risk and
the development of mitigation strategies to support these groups.

Age
Children, especially in the youngest age groups, often cannot protect themselves during a
disaster because they lack the necessary resources, knowledge, or life experiences to

  3-7

  Page 117 of 346
   2026 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan | City of La Verne Profile

effectively cope with the situation. Hazard mitigation planning needs to be tailored such that
the community is prepared to ensure that children are safe during disaster events and that
families with children have access to necessary information and tools.

People 65 years old and older are likely to require financial support, transportation, medical
care, or assistance with ordinary daily activities, especially during disasters. They are more
likely to be vision, hearing, and/or mobility impaired, more likely to experience mental
impairment or dementia, and more likely to live in assisted-living facilities where emergency
preparedness is at the discretion of facility operators. Hazard mitigation needs to account
for such needs.

Poverty
Economically disadvantaged families have limited ability to absorb losses due to hazard
impacts. Wealth enables families to absorb and recover from losses more quickly, due to
insurance, savings, and often the availability of low-cost credit. People with lower incomes
tend not to have access to these resources. At the same time, poorer families are likely to
inhabit poor quality housing and reside in locations that are most vulnerable to hazard
events. Economically disadvantaged neighborhoods are also likely to have relatively poor
infrastructure and facilities, which exacerbate the disaster consequences for community
members who live there.

Linguistic Isolation
For populations who experience linguistic isolation due to limited English proficiency, disaster
communication may be difficult, especially in communities for whom translators and
accurate translations of advisories may be scarce. Such households are likely to rely on
relatives and local social networks (i.e., friends and neighbors) for information for preparing
for a disaster event.

People of Color
Social and economic marginalization of certain racial and ethnic groups, including real
estate discrimination, has resulted in greater vulnerability of these groups to all types of
hazards. Based on data from a number of studies, African Americans, Native Americans, and
populations of Asian, Pacific Islander, or Hispanic origin are likely to be more vulnerable than
the broader community. Research shows that minorities are less likely to be involved in pre-
disaster planning and experience higher mortality rates during disaster events. Post-disaster
recovery often exhibits cultural insensitivity. Since higher proportions of ethnic minorities live
below the poverty line than the majority white population, poverty can compound
vulnerability.

Renters
Renters are more vulnerable to natural disasters due to factors like less access to insurance,
greater financial strain in moving, and potential displacement challenges in the aftermath.
They also may live in less resilient housing and face delays in property repairs, hindering
recovery efforts.

People Who Rely on Public Transportation
Residents who do not own a vehicle may need additional assistance during evacuation from
severe hazard events. Disruptions to transit systems can hinder evacuation efforts.

Access and Functional Needs
Persons with disabilities or other access and functional needs are more likely to have
difficulty responding to a hazard event than the general population. Family, neighbors, and
local government are the first level of response to assist these individuals, and coordination
of efforts to meet their access and functional needs is paramount to life safety efforts.
Emergency managers need to distinguish between functional and medical needs to plan for
incidents that require evacuation and sheltering. Knowing the percentage of population with
access and functional needs allows emergency management personnel and first
responders to anticipate the services needed by that population.

 3.4.3  Development Trends

Future Trends
La Verne is a largely built-out community with limited vacant land. Desirable new growth
consistent with the Community Vision is directed along the City’s key corridors (Foothill
Boulevard and Arrow Highway) and around its major activity and business centers (Old Town
La Verne, the Metro A Line Station, La Verne Business Park, and Brackett Field) (City of La Verne
2025). As a mostly built-out city, La Verne has a relatively limited capacity for new
development. Population growth is anticipated to follow current trends as noted in Section
3.3.1, with future development trends focusing redevelopment and infill development.
Because the City has finite options for expanding the local economic base, each future
development project takes on a high level of importance in terms of meeting the City’s
economic development goals.

Planning Framework
Future growth and redevelopment in the City of La Verne will be directed by its General Plan.
As a growth Management state, the State of California mandates that all cities and Counties
develop and adopt General Plans. California Government Code 65041.1 established state
planning priorities which are intended to promote equity, strengthen the economy, protect
the environment, and promote public health and safety in the state, including in urban,
suburban, and rural communities, shall be as follows:

  1.  To promote infill development and equity by rehabilitating, maintaining, and
  improving existing infrastructure that supports infill development and appropriate
  reuse and redevelopment of previously developed, underutilized land that is presently
  served by transit, streets, water, sewer, and other essential services, particularly in
  under-served areas, and to preserving cultural and historic resources.
  2. To protect environmental and agricultural resources by protecting, preserving, and
  enhancing the state's most valuable natural resources; natural lands such as
  wetlands, watersheds, wildlife habitats, and other wildlands; recreation lands such as
  parks, trails, greenbelts, and other open space; and landscapes with locally unique
  features and areas identified by the state as deserving special protection.
  3. To encourage efficient development patterns by ensuring that any infrastructure
  associated with development, other than infill development, supports new
  development that does all of the following:
  a. Uses land efficiently.
  b. Is built adjacent to existing developed areas to the extent consistent with the
  priorities specified pursuant to subdivision.
  c. Is located in an area appropriately planned for growth.

5.  RISK ASSESSMENT METHODOLOGY AND TOOLS
5.1  ASSESSING RISK

In hazard mitigation planning, risk is the potential for damage or loss when natural hazards
interact with people or assets, such as buildings, infrastructure, and resources. A risk
assessment is a process used to identify potential hazards and analyze what could happen
if a disaster or hazard occurs. It involves a data-driven analysis to identify potential hazards,
what could happen if hazards occur, and determine vulnerabilities to hazards (FEMA 2023).

The risk assessment process focuses on three main elements – hazard identification,
exposure identification, and vulnerability identification and loss estimation.

5.2  RISK ASSESSMENT TOOLS

  Local Plan Requirement A4 – 44 CFR Part 201.6(b)(3)

  Review and incorporation, if appropriate, of existing plans, studies, reports, and technical
  information.
For this LHMP, GIS and FEMA’s Hazus software programs were used to conduct the risk
assessment.

 5.2.1  Mapping

GIS tools provide a mechanism to perform quantitative analysis. Hazards that have specified
geographic boundaries permit analysis using GIS. These hazards include the following:

  •  Dam Failure
  •  Earthquake
  •  Flood
  •  Landslide
  •  Wildfire

 5.2.2  Modeling

FEMA’s Hazus model version 6.1 was used to evaluate the following hazards:

  •  Dam Failure—A Level 2 user-defined analysis was performed for general building stock
  and critical facilities and infrastructure in inundation areas. Potential losses for the
  combined inundation areas of multiple dams, specific dams noted later in this section,
  were estimated using the Hazus flood module. To estimate damage that would result
  from a flood, Hazus uses pre-defined relationships between flood depth at a structure

  5-1

  Page 138 of 346
   2026 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan | Risk Assessment Methodology and
  Tools

  and resulting damage, with damage given as a percent of total replacement value.
  Curves defining these relationships have been developed for damage to structures
  and for damage to typical contents within a structure. By inputting inundation depth
  data, estimated first floor elevations, and known property replacement cost values,
  dollar-value estimates of damage were generated.
  •  Earthquake—A Level 2 analysis was performed to assess earthquake exposure and
  vulnerability for three deterministic scenarios: Cucamonga M6.88, S. San Andreas
  M7.91, and Sierra Madre M7.16. The Hazus methodology uses ground motion and
  ground failure fragility curves to estimate damage state probabilities which are then
  used to estimate losses at the structure level.

Overview
FEMA developed the Hazards U.S., or Hazus, model in 1997 to estimate losses caused by
earthquakes and identify areas that face the highest risk and potential for loss. Hazus was
later expanded into a multi-hazard methodology with new models for estimating potential
losses from hurricanes and floods. The use of Hazus for hazard mitigation planning offers
numerous advantages:

  •  Provides a consistent methodology for assessing risk across geographic and political
  entities.
  •  Provides a way to save data so that it can readily be updated as population, inventory,
  and other factors change and as mitigation planning efforts evolve.
  •  Facilitates the review of mitigation plans because it helps to ensure that FEMA
  methodologies are incorporated.
  •  Supports grant applications by calculating benefits using FEMA definitions and
  terminology.
  •  Produces hazard data and loss estimates that can be used in communication with
  local stakeholders.
  •  Is administered by the local government and can be used to manage and update a
  LHMP throughout its implementation.

Hazus is a GIS-based software program used to support risk assessments, mitigation
planning, and emergency planning and response. It provides a wide range of inventory data,
such as demographics, building stock, community lifelines, transportation and utility lifeline,
and multiple models to estimate potential losses from natural disasters. The program can
be used to map hazard data and the results of damage and economic loss estimates for
buildings and infrastructure.

Level of Detail for Evaluation
Hazus provides default data for inventory, vulnerability and hazards; this default data can be
supplemented with local data to provide a more refined analysis. The model can carry out
three levels of analysis, depending on the format and level of detail of information about the
Planning Area:

  •  Level 1—All of the information needed to produce an estimate of losses is included in
  the software’s default data. This data is derived from national databases and
  describes in general terms the characteristic parameters of the Planning Area.
  •  Level 2—More accurate estimates of losses require more detailed information about
  the Planning Area. To produce Level 2 estimates of losses, detailed information is
  required about local geology, hydrology, hydraulics and building inventory, as well as
  data about utilities and critical facilities. This information is needed in a GIS format.
  •  Level 3—This level of analysis generates the most accurate estimate of losses. It
  requires detailed engineering and geotechnical information to customize it for the
  Planning Area.

5.3  RISK ASSESSMENT APPROACH

This plan evaluated risks associated with each identified hazard for La Verne. Each hazard
was profiled using the following steps:

  •  Description of the Hazard: Defining the hazard and a discussion of potential impacts.
  •  Location: Geographic areas most affected by the hazard.
  •  Extent: Measuring the intensity of the hazard, warning time for preparations, and the
  reasonable worst-case scenario.
  •  Previous Occurrences: Summary of past events that have impacted the Planning Area.
  •  Future Occurrences: Probability estimates, including potential frequency and intensity
  shifts caused by climate change and population and development trends.

For each hazard, one of the following assessment approaches was used, depending on the
type of information available for the hazard:

  •  Quantitative assessment—Performed when numerical data are available to define
  risk. Available numerical hazard data may include financial impact and probability.
  •  Qualitative assessment—Uses words to describe and categorize the likelihood and
  consequences of a risk when numerical data are unavailable.

Vulnerability of exposed structures and infrastructure was evaluated by estimating the
probability of occurrence of each event and assessing structures, facilities, and systems that
are exposed to each hazard.

5.4  SOURCES OF DATA USED IN RISK ASSESSMENT

Hazard information and data were collected for all hazards from a variety of sources,
described in the sections below.

 5.4.1  Building and Cost Data

Parcel and building information from the Los Angeles County Assessor were used to compile
a detailed, citywide structure inventory including replacement costs. Replacement cost is the
cost to replace the entire structure with one of equal quality and utility. Replacement cost is
based on industry-standard cost-estimation models published in RS Means Square Foot
Costs (RS Means, 2024). It is calculated using the RS Means square foot cost for a structure,
which is based on the Hazus occupancy class (i.e., multi-family residential or commercial
retail trade), multiplied by the square footage of the structure from the tax assessor data.
The construction class and number of stories for single-family residential structures also
factor into determining the square foot costs.

 5.4.2  Community Lifelines

An inventory of critical facilities and infrastructure was compiled from City, county, state, and
national datasets. The facilities were categorized by FEMA’s Community Lifelines: Safety and
Security;  Food,  Hydration,  Shelter;  Health  and  Medical;  Energy;  Communications;
Transportation; Hazardous Material; and Water Systems. To protect individual privacy and
the security of assets, information is presented in aggregate, without details about specific
individual properties or facilities.

 5.4.3  Population

The CDC’s SVI dataset was used for the population analysis. In alignment with the California
State HMP, an overall index value of 0.7 or greater was used to define the socially vulnerable
population. In preparation for spatial overlays with the hazard data, the spatial extent of the
Census tract-level SVI data was refined to include populated areas only. The SVI data was
combined with the dasymetric Census block data from Hazus to adjust the tract boundaries
to populated areas.

5.5  DATA LIMITATIONS

Loss estimates, exposure assessments, and hazard-specific vulnerability evaluations rely on
the best available data and methodologies. Uncertainties are inherent in any loss estimation
methodology and arise in part from incomplete scientific knowledge concerning natural
hazards and their effects on the built environment.

Uncertainties also result from the following:

  •  Approximations and simplifications necessary to conduct such a study.
  •  Incomplete or dated inventory, demographic, or economic parameter data.
  •  The unique nature, geographic extent, and severity of each hazard.
  •  Mitigation measures already employed by the participating municipalities.
  •  The amount of advance notice residents have to prepare for a specific hazard event.
  •  Uncertainty of climate change projections.

Hazus currently represents the industry best management practice for assessing risk in
support of hazard mitigation planning. However, the Hazus model is limited by the availability
of data to support its working components. The model makes assumptions where firm data
are not available. Assumptions are used, for example, to estimate ground deformation
caused by liquefaction. These model limitations can lead to an understatement or
overstatement of risk.

These factors can result in a range of uncertainty in loss estimates, possibly by a factor of
two or more. Therefore, potential exposure and loss estimates are approximate. These results
do not predict precise results and should be used to understand relative risk. Over the long
term, the City of La Verne will collect additional data to update and refine existing inventories
to assist in estimating potential losses.

6.1  HAZARD PROFILE

  Local Plan Requirement B1 – 44 CFR Part 201.6(c)(2)(i)

  Include a description of the type, location, and extent for the identified hazards of

 6.1.1  Description of the Hazard

Definition and Classification of Dams
A dam is an artificial barrier that can store water, wastewater, or liquid-borne materials for
many reasons—flood control, human water supply, irrigation, livestock water supply, energy
generation, containment of mine tailings, recreation, or pollution control. Many dams fulfill a
combination of these functions. They are an important resource in the United States. In
California, dams are regulated by the State of California Division of Safety of Dams. Additional
regulatory oversight of dams is cited in Chapter 15 and described in Appendix C (Federal &
State Agencies, Programs & Regulations).

The California Water Code (Division 3) defines a dam as any artificial barrier, together with
appurtenant works, that does or may impound or divert water, and that either:

  •  Has a height of more than 6 feet and it impounds 50 acre-feet or more of water, or
  •  Has a height of 25 feet or higher and impounds more than 15 acre-feet of water.

Dams can be classified according to their purpose, the construction material or methods
used, their slope or cross section, the way they resist the force of the water pressure, or the
means used for controlling seepage. Materials used to construct dams include earth, rock,
tailings from mining or milling, concrete, masonry, steel, timber, plastic, rubber, and
combinations of these.

Cause of the Hazard
Partial or full failure of dams has the potential to cause massive destruction to the
ecosystems and communities located downstream. Partial or full failure can occur because
of one or a combination of the following reasons (FEMA 2016):

  •  Overtopping caused by floods that exceed the dam capacity (inadequate spillway
  capacity).
  •  Prolonged periods of rainfall and flooding.
  •  Deliberate acts of sabotage (terrorism).

  6-1

  Page 146 of 346
   2026 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan | Dam Failure

  •  Structural failure of materials used in dam construction.
  •  Movement and/or failure of the foundation supporting the dam.
  •  Settlement and cracking of concrete or embankment dams.
  •  Piping and internal erosion of soil in embankment dams.
  •  Inadequate or negligent operation, maintenance, and upkeep.
  •  Failure of upstream dams on the same waterway.
  •  Earthquake (liquefaction/landslides).

Many dam failures in the United States have been secondary results of other disasters. The
most common causes are earthquakes, landslides, extreme storms, equipment malfunction,
structural damage, foundation failures, and sabotage. Poor construction, lack of
maintenance and repair, and deficient operational procedures are preventable or
correctable by a program of regular inspections. Terrorism and vandalism are serious
concerns that all operators of public facilities must plan for; these threats are under
continuous review by public safety agencies.

Planning Requirements

State of California
All dams whose inundation areas may impact the Planning Area have emergency action
plans (EAPs) on file. The EAPs must include the following (Cal OES 2021):

  •  Emergency notification flow charts.
  •  Information on a four-step response process.
  •  Description of agencies’ roles and actions in response to an emergency incident.
  •  Description of actions to be taken in advance of an emergency.
  •  Inundation maps.
  •  Additional information such as revision records and distribution lists.

After the EAPs are approved by the state, the law requires dam owners to send the approved
EAPs to relevant stakeholders. Local public agencies can then adopt emergency procedures
that incorporate the information in the EAP in a manner that conforms to local needs and
includes methods and procedures for alerting and warning the public and other response
and preparedness related items (Cal OES 2021).

Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
Dams that fall under the jurisdiction of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC)
also have specified planning requirements. FERC has the largest dam safety program in the
United States. It cooperates with a large number of federal and state agencies to ensure and
promote dam safety and, more recently, homeland security. FERC requires licensees to
prepare EAPs and conducts training sessions on how to develop and test these plans. The

plans are designed to serve as an early warning system if there is a potential for, or a sudden
release of water from, a dam failure or accident to the dam. The plans include operational
procedures that may be used, such as reducing reservoir levels and downstream flows and
procedures for notifying affected residents and agencies responsible for emergency
management. These plans are frequently updated and tested to ensure that in emergency
situations everyone knows what to do, thus saving lives and minimizing property damage.

FEMA Guidance for Flood Mapping
FEMA’s Federal Guidelines for Inundation Mapping of Flood Risks Associated with Dam
Incidents and Failures is part of the National Dam Safety Program, a partnership of states,
federal agencies, and other stakeholders formed to encourage individual and community
responsibility for dam safety. Under this program, states are responsible for regulating non-
federal dams. The guidelines provide information for federal and state agencies, local
governments, dam owners, and emergency management officials to use for reducing flood
hazards and the resulting potential for economic damage and loss of life. It is a resource for
developing state-specific guidelines for dam safety and as a reference manual for mapping
dam breach inundation zones (FEMA 2013).

Rehabilitation of High Hazard Potential Dams
FEMA’s Rehabilitation of High Hazard Potential Dams grant program provides assistance for
eligible rehabilitation activities that reduce dam risk and increase community preparedness.
For the purposes of the HHPD program, the term “rehabilitation” means the repair,
replacement, reconstruction, or removal of a dam that is carried out to meet applicable state
dam safety and security standards (FEMA 2020).

 6.1.3  Extent

Measuring Intensity
The increased risk or susceptibility to dam failure can be determined through inundation
zones. The “inundation zone” is the area downstream of the dam that would be flooded in the
event of a failure or uncontrolled release of water and is generally much larger than the area
for the normal river or stream flood event. The “dam breach inundation zone” is larger than
the 100-year floodplain used on FEMA’s flood insurance rate maps (FIRMs) (FEMA 2013).

Warning Time
Warning time for dam failure depends on the cause of the failure. In events of extreme
precipitation or massive snowmelt, evacuations can be planned with sufficient time. In the
event of a structural failure due to earthquake, it is possible that there would be no warning
time. The USGS Earthquake Hazards Program has several dam-safety related earthquake
programs, including dam-specific earthquake monitoring programs in California to help
monitor safety concerns following seismic events.

A dam’s structural type affects warning time. Earthen dams do not tend to fail completely or
instantaneously. Once a breach is initiated, discharging water erodes the breach until the
reservoir is empty or the erosion stops. Concrete dams also tend to begin with a partial
breach. The time of breach formation ranges from a few minutes to a few hours (U.S. Army
Corps of Engineers 2025).

Worst-Case Scenario
A worst-case dam failure scenario for the City of La Verne would be the “probable maximum
flood” for the combined dams. The probable maximum flood is defined as the flood that may
be expected from the most severe combination of critical meteorological and hydrologic
conditions.

Summary of Significant Events

1963 Baldwin Hills Reservoir Collapse
On December 14, 1963, the dam at the head of Cloverdale Road broke in the Baldwin Hills
section of Los Angeles. A river of rushing water from the broken dam resulted in lost homes,
ruined property, and even death. Automobiles, fragments of houses, and chunks of concrete
were carried along the flood’s path and deposited on the ruins of Village Green. A helicopter
team rescued 18 people.

Climate Change
Probability of dam failure could increase with changing climate conditions. Increases in the
frequency and intensity of extreme rain events could increase the probability that dams will
fail or overtop. Although dam failure is not considered a direct result of a changing climate,
changes in climate can impact the functionality of dam’s infrastructure. And/or the
operation of dams. All dam operations are based on hydrographs. As the hydrographs
change, dam operations will change. The 2017 Oroville Dam Spillway incident is a perfect
example of how increased precipitation associated with climate change impacts affected
dam operations.

Potential Future Impacts
The future impacts from dam failure on the City of La Verne are not anticipated to increase
since the current impacts are so negligible. If operational procedures for the Santa Fe dam
are adjusted the probability of occurrence for these negligible impacts could change, but
the extent and location of the hazard would not change. While the City is completely built out
